abstract:
The widespread use
of pesticides, particularly in combinations,
has resulted in enhanced hazardous health effects. However, little
is known about their molecular mechanism of interactions. The aim
of this study was to assess the neurotoxicity effect of pesticides
in mixtures by adopting a 3D in vitro developed neurospheroid model,
followed by treatment by increased concentrations of pesticides for
24 h and analysis by a shotgun proteomic-based approach with high-resolution
tandem mass spectrometry. Three proteins, namely, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate-dehydrogenase
(GAPDH), α-enolase, and phosphoglycerate-kinase-1, were selected
as key targets in the metabolic process. Only high doses of pesticides
mitigated cell-density proliferation with the occurrence of apoptotic
cells, which unlikely makes any neurological alterations in environmental
regulatory exposures. The proteomic analysis showed that majority
of altered proteins were implicated in cell metabolism. De novo peptide
sequencing revealed ion losses and adduct formation, namely, a trityl-post-translational
modification in the active site of 201-GAPDH protein. The study also
highlights the plausible role of pyrethroids to be implicated in the
deleterious effects of pesticides in a mixture. To the best of our
knowledge, our finding is the first in toxicoproteomics to deeply
elucidate pesticides’ molecular interactions and their ability
to adduct proteins as a pivotal role in the neurotoxicity mechanism.

The Declaration

The target participants consented

2.3
Sample Collection and Culture Conditions
Preliminary experiments have been conducted on diverse meningiomas
[human brain meningiomas (MNGs)] histological subtypes including meningiomal
metastasis in order to access the neurotoxicity effect of our selected
pesticide molecules and determine the inhibitory concentration (IC
50
) of the binary mixture. Nine surgical specimens were used
for the generation of neurospheroids that were grown in triplicate
by applying enzymatic and nonenzymatic dissociation techniques as
detailed in the Supporting Information file.
Afterward, to evaluate
the MNG self-renewal ability to form secondary subspheres, primary
spheres were gently dissociated into single cells, plated into a single-cell
ultralow attachment plate, and maintained in the neural stem cell
culture medium.
We visually inspected spheroid health and growth
under an inverted
phase contrast bright-field microscope (MOTIC AE21, Motic Incorporation
Ltd. Hong Kong, China) equipped with an Axiocam camera 208, the main
characteristics of which are described in our previously published
studies.
64
,
65
2.4
Immunohistochemical Staining
Primary
cell identity was confirmed prior to use by immunohistochemical (IHC)
staining, namely, for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) (Bio-Rad cat.
no. MCA1908, RRID: AB_322557) and vimentin (VIM) (Abcam catalog no.
4211–1, RRID: AB_765097), which are the most widely used markers
of MNG diagnosis, and keratin (RayBiotech cat. no. DS-MB-01725, RRID:
AB_854575) and GATA3 (trans-acting T-cell-specific transcription factor)
(BD Biosciences catalog no. 563349, RRID: AB_2738152) for the diagnosis
of meningiomal metastasis.
Neurospheroid expression of “Stemness”
markers was also analyzed for CD133, VIM, Nestin, SOX2, GFAP (glial
fibrillary acidic protein) and βIII-tubulin using the same panels
of mouse-anti-human monoclonal primary antibodies as performed in
our previous studies on gliomas and medulloblastoma brain tumors.
64
,
65
Following standard fixation and embedding techniques, both
primary
cells and 3D spheroids were extracted and processed into histological
blocks and then sectioned into very thin slides for IHC staining.
The detailed experimental protocol is presented in the Supporting
Information file.
2.5
Pesticide Treatment
We have adopted
the same method described in our previous published works
64
−
66
for in vitro neurotoxicity analysis of pesticide mixtures on human
stem-cell-derived 3D-neuronal spheroids. We daily assessed the neurospheroid
health and growth size by microscopy, and after 7 days, once the diameter
reached the ideal range of 250 to 350 μm, we measured the coefficient
of variation (CV) (Appendices eqs A and B) in spheroid volumes to
confirm growth uniformity and size reproducibility prior pesticide
treatment.
Since tumor cells are typically less sensitive in
3D compounds compared to 2D compounds, many trials have been performed
to check the appraite inhibitory concentrations (IC
50
)
of our pesticide molecules used in a binary mixture.
Five serial
diluted concentrations were used ranging from 2.95
μM (754 ng/g) to 0.59 mM (151 × 10
3
ng/g) of
IMD and 0.55 μM (247 ng/g) to 0.11 mM (49.5 ng/g) of λ-CYH.
After careful removal of 100 μL of neurosphere medium from each
plate and adding 100 μL of pesticide mixture, we kept the plates
in a humidified incubator at 5% CO2/37 °C for 24 h. For each
concentration, three replicates were analyzed. Each analysis also
included untreated control cells, obtained by substituting 100 μL
of media with 100 μL of 0.01% DMSO. At the end of the exposure
period, toxicity end points were established for both exposed and
control neurospheroids.
2.6
Spheroid Viability Tracking
The MTT
assay and microscopy were used for the assessment of the histopathological
profile and morphological alterations of tumor tissues.
2.6.1
MTT Assay Viability
After 24 h
of pesticide treatment, the MTT assay viability was performed following
the protocol described in our previous published works.
64
,
65
A dose–response curve was created, and a nonlinear regression
analysis was used to determine the IC
50
value of the mixture
of IMD and λ-CYH (concentrations needed for 50% growth inhibition).
2.6.2
Assessing Morphological Changes
The morphological
changes in the spheroid shape and density after
pesticide exposure were evaluated by microscopy.
2.6.3
Histopathological Profile Analysis
This method was
adopted for assessment of the cytotoxic response
based on cell proliferation of tumor neurospheroids following pesticide
treatment. The collected pieces of tumor tissues were manipulated
following the protocol described in our previous published studies.
64
,
65
2.7
Measurement of Glycolytic Activity
Brain tumor samples from the control and treated spheroids were collected
and washed with cold PBS solution, then suspended in ice-cold 100
mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4), and centrifuged for 10 min
at 3000 rpm at 4 °C using a cold microcentrifuge. The supernatant
homogenates were collected for the estimation of the glycolytic activity
by colorimetric methods using standard commercial kits such as human
glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate-dehydrogenase (GAPDH) activity assay kit
(ab204732), Enolase assay kit (ab241024), and phosphoglycerate kinase
activity assay kit (ab252890), which are all from BioVision (Abcam,
USA). Assays for each enzyme were performed by following the kit protocol.
Enzyme activity is expressed as U/mg of total protein in the sample.
2.8
Sample Preparation and Protein Extraction
Following a 24 h pesticide treatment period, three samples of each
treated and nontretaed brain tumor spheroids were processed in the
same way to the detailed protocol described in our published studies
64
,
65
for protein extraction, reduction, alkylation, and trypsin digestion.
The resulting extracted peptides were lyophilized to near-dryness
to be analyzed by the nano-ultrahigh performance liquid chromatography
(UHPLC)-MS/MS.
2.9
Analysis by Nanoflow UHPLC-MS/MS
Samples were analyzed on the same day by high-resolution tandem
mass
spectrometry consisting of an Ultimate 3000 nano-UHPLC system (ThermoFisher
Scientific, USA), an ESI nanospray source, a Q-Exactive HF mass spectrometer
(Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), and a higher energy collision induced
dissociation (HCD) fragmentation mode. The nanocolumn comprised a
trapping column (PepMap C18, 100 Å, 100 μm × 2 cm,
5 μm) and an analytical column (PepMap C18, 100 Å, 75 μm
× 50 cm, 2 μm). We adopted the same analytical conditions
and the same mobile phase as performed in our previous works on glioma
and medulloblastoma human brain tumors,
64
,
65
which are
described in this associated data repository.
2.10
Data-MS
Analysis and Protein Identification
Based on the species
of our investigated samples, we have applied
the same MaxQuant research engine and the same setting parameters,
as performed in our previous works on glioma and medulloblastoma human
brain tumors
64
,
65
and supplied in the associated
data repository.
Proteins containing at least one identified
peptide were detected at a high confidence interval (95%). A threshold
of a false discovery rate (FDR) of ≤0.05 was applied to compare
the proteome profiles between the two groups and judge the significance
of the differences in protein expression maps. Only proteins identified
three times were taken into account.
Based on log
2
FC criteria and paired
t
test with a
P
value threshold of 0.05, the proteins
were filtered into two groups: “up-regulation” with
positive values and “down-regulation” with negative
values.

Screening of Protein-Adduct Formation by
De Novo Sequencing
Protein adductomics was performed by the
same strategy adopted in our previously published work on medulloblastoma
human brain tumors.
65
The procedure
of manual verification was applied for the validation of adduct compounds
based on their added mass shift (Δ
M
).
The full workflow schematic illustration of our adaptive strategy
for protein adductomics and/or PTMs is shown in
Figure
2
.
Figure 2
Schematic illustration of the workflow by an
untargeted bottom-up
proteomic-approach-based MS analysis for the identification of protein-PTMs.
DDA, data-dependent acquisition mode; HCD, higher energy collisional
dissociation; MS1/MS2, tandem mass spectrometry; FDR, false discovery
rate; FC, fold change.
2.12
Bioinformatic
Analysis
As performed
in our previous study on glioma brain tumors,
64
we adopted the same databases for the analysis of our differentially
expressed proteins, namely, PANTHER (version 17.0) for the gene ontology
(GO) enrichment analysis,
67
METASCAPE
68
,
69
for pathway enrichment analysis, and STRING (Search Tool for the
Retrieval of Interacting Genes/Proteins) database (version 11.0)
70
for the identification of the most encoding
hub genes by Protein–protein Interaction (PPI) network analysis.

Other Statistical Analyses
Data
by GraphPad Prism Software (Version.8, San Diego, CA, USA) were expressed
as mean values with ± standard deviation (SD), and the statistical
significance of differences between counts was determined by the unpaired
Student’s
t
test. Three duplicates were conducted
for each distinct experiment.
P
values ≤0.05
were statistically significant.

body:
1
Introduction
In agricultural areas,
pesticides are the most widely used chemicals,
especially in mixtures, due to the necessity to increase efficacy
and reduce the cost of crop pest treatment. However, because of lack
of safe management in developing countries, various environmental
compartments are contaminated and pesticide residues are found in
a wide range of everyday foods resulting in enhanced toxicity for
various organisms,
1
−
10
especially if they are simultaneously exposed to more than two chemical
substances that may interact and have synergistic effects, leading
to many health problems such as cancer, chronic inflammatory diseases,
and neurological disorders.
11
−
15
The use of synthetic pyrethroids in combination with neonicotinoid
insecticides is common in modern agricultural practices, given that
diverse methylcarbamate and organophosphorus pesticides have been
now subjected to restrictions as they are highly toxic to mammals
and ineffective against pest resistance.
16
,
17
In our Tunisian market, mixtures based on imidacloprid (IMD), a
member of the neonicotinoid class, and Lambda-cyhalothrin (λ-CYH),
a new generation type II synthetic pyrethroid, are most widely used
owing to their high efficacy and broad spectrum practices
18
with lowest toxicity to mammals and birds.
11
,
19
−
22
Previous toxicological studies had been conducted to examine each
pesticide’s possible neurotoxic effects on nontargeted organisms,
including animals,
23
−
30
aquatic creatures (fish, carps),
31
,
32
or in mixtures,
33
−
35
and to assess their oxidative damage, metabolic impairment, genotoxicity,
and endocrine-disrupting activity
17
,
36
−
41
· Nevertheless, little is known about the corresponding neurotoxicity
molecular mechanisms, and even studies on their plausible interacting
effects on human neuroglial cells are lacking.
Pesticides are
known to induce toxicity at the cellular level through
alteration in redox homeostasis by the generation of oxidative stress
following the overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS)
42
either by products of detoxification pathways,
altering the functioning of mitochondrial transport and endoplasmic
reticulum electron chains, or by entering redox cycles.
43
−
48
Disruption of the normal cell state can deregulate several signaling
pathways,
49
impair neuroeffector junctions,
50
−
54
or harm all cell components such as proteins, DNA, and lipids, resulting
in lipid peroxidation, metabolism disruption due to variation in the
expression of antioxidants, inactivation of glycolytic enzymes, and
ultimately to apoptotic or necrotic cell death.
55
−
59
Proteins as one of the major targets of oxygen-free
radicals and
other reactive species may encounter post-translational modifications
(PTMs) or be covalently modified by adduct formation on its key amino
acid side chains to initiate toxicity via modification of their structure
and/or cellular function (e.g., catalytic activity) to secondarily
damage the cytological processes.
60
These
modifications are considered pivotal predictors of toxicity or biomarkers
to diagnose chemical poisoning or examine exposure to toxicants which
allows detailed understanding of the underlying mechanisms involved
in toxicity.
60
Characterization of
protein adducts and/or PTMs that symbolizes
changes in the polypeptide chain has received great research interest
as a potential diagnostic biomarker related to toxic response for
an in-depth identification of their role in pathogenesis, which helps
answer clinical questions on novel strategies of diagnosis and therapy.
However, their analysis is challenging which highlights the need for
computational and sensitive methods for their detection.
61
Cultured cell lines in toxicology studies
have been well recognized
and widely used, especially the 3D proliferation of primary cells,
which is considered as the most rigorous and representative model
for in vitro cytotoxicity investigations that could bridge the gap
between animal models, which require the use of a high number without
being a true representative of the human body,
28
and conventional 2D monolayer cell cultures, which cannot
mimic the intricacy and diversity of clinical tumors developed according
to a particular structure and architecture.
The use of in vitro
models with proteomics approaches has recently
grown in cancer-biology science due to the advancement in modern mass
spectrometry (MS) including new ionization techniques, fragmentation
methods, and more sensitive and accurate analyzers, as well as improvement
of enrichment strategies, development of more powerful PTM workflows
by targeted or semitargeted scanning procedures, bioinformatics tools,
and powerful algorithms of protein search databases. Hence, it is
now possible to perform the identification of various PTMs and protein-xenobiotic
adducts with high sensitivity and accuracy into a single measurement
62
,
63
·
Hence, the current study was designed to explore whether
low or
high doses of IMD and λ-CYH used in the mixture could elicit
neural cell apoptosis in order to assess their potential neurotoxicity
and identify novel molecular mechanisms. Our strategy first involved
development of human stem-cell-derived 3D-neuronal spheroids for in
vitro neurotoxicity analysis after short-term treatments with pesticides
in binary mixtures. Afterward, we adopted a shotgun-proteomic-based
approach for the identification of protein-PTMs and prediction of
alteration sites. The full workflow adaptive methodogy is described
in
Figure
1
.
Figure 1
Diagram illustrating
the adaptive methodology for the identification
of protein-PTMs using an untargeted bottom-up approach on 3D-stem-cell-derived
neuronal spheroids from MNGs.

Results
3.1
Characteristics of Selected Patients
MNGs derived from
arachnoid cells were the most common intracranial
tumor for our patients hospitalized in the neurosurgery department
of Habib Bourguiba Medium Hospital. Although, grade I represents the
most frequent type of MNGs, we have tried in our analysis to conduct
a homogenate study by selecting all histopathological grades based
on the WHO classification: grade I (benign), II (atypical), and III
(malignant and the most aggressive forms associated with the highest
risk of recurrence and shortest survival times).
Thus, all patients who participated
in this study were exposed to image examinations, such as magnetic
resonance images pre- and postsurgery for the identification and evaluation
of tumor recurrence.
Nine freshly resected human specimens were
collected from patients
diagnosed with MNGs grade I, II, and III. Demographics and clinical
characteristics of patients are summarized in Supplementary
Table S1
.

Measurement of Glycolytic Activity
We examined the
biochemical changes in terms of the glycolytic activity
for three enzymes, namely, GAPDH, α-enolase (ENO1), and phosphoglycerate-kinase-1
(PGK1), in order to validate and make evidence of the cytotoxicity
effect of pesticides to induce metabolic perturbation.
The adopted
commercial activity assay kit provides simple and sensitive colorimetric
methods for monitoring enzymes’ glycolytic activity in various
samples. In this assay, GAPDH catalyzes the conversion of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
to 1,3-bisphosphate glycerate and an intermediate, which reacts with
a developer to form a colored product that absorbs maximally at 450
nm. The enolase activity is determined following the consumption of

and required substrates. The consumption of NADH was monitored as
a decrease in absorbance at 340 nm. For the PGK1 activity, in the
first step of the enzymatic assay, PGK converts 3-phosphoglycerate
and ATP to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and ADP. The nascent intermediate
was detected via a series of enzymatic reactions that lead to the
oxidation of NADH to NAD+, which can be easily detected.

4
Discussion
4.1
Isolation of Tumor Stemlike Cells from Human
Meningiomas and Characterization of Sphere Formation and Stemness
Markers
Cancer stemlike cells, often referred as tumor-initiating
cells,
71
−
80
are issued from cultured human brain tumor that could proliferate
and generate clusters of multipotent floating cells called neurospheres.
80
These developed 3D spheroids constitute an advanced
and exciting in vitro model for cytotoxicity studies and drug discovery
since they yield more biologically meaningful data than the traditional
2D monolayer cultures. In fact, spheroids contain a mixture of neuronal,
astrocytes, and endothelia cells, which set up the vascular network
structures and mimic the brain tissue.
80
In our study, we have begun setting up primary cell cultures
by using a serum-free neurosphere medium in order to maintain the
same properties as the primary tumor and avoiding spontaneous cell
differentiation.
66
,
81
Then, we developed 3D stem-cell-derived
neuronal spheroids (primary spheroids) to yield finally to secondary
neurospheres or subspheres.
The cytotoxicity studies were achieved
after 7 days of neurospheroids’
growth once they reached size around 250–350 μm of diameter,
which is reported as the optimal size than 500 μm to enable
drug perfusion and avoid necrotic centers and hypoxic regions.
78
,
79
Furthermore, as performed in our previous studies,
64
,
65
since the spheroids’ volume and shape are among the critical
parameters that influence data variability, we accurately measured
the CV of spheroids’ volume on day 7 by using the Image-Pro
Analyzer software as an improved substituted method to cytometers
79
in order to select homogeneous spheroids, minimizing
difference in cells’ responses to chemicals, and hence to acquire
reliable results.
Tumor stemlike cells are characterized by
their spherical shape,
unlimited proliferation, or self-renewal to secondary neurospheres,
as well as the expression patterns of stemlike markers specific to
their parent tumor.
82
Hence, we have elected
to examine their expression of CD133, Nestin, VIM, SOX2, GFAP, and
βIII-tubulin.
Interestingly, CD133
i
s
the most commonly used
marker for cancer stemlike cells that is related to cell proliferation
and differentiation of various malignancies.
83
,
84
Nestin, a type VI intermediate filament, is an important cancer
stem cells marker for central nervous system (CNS) tumor growth, migration,
and invasion,
85
,
86
detected at higher levels in
grades II and III MNGs compared to grade I.
87
The transcription factor SOX2 has been observed in several CNS tumors
cancer stem cells.
84
,
86
,
88
VIM is highly associated with MNGs. It is a class III intermediate
protein expressed in mesenchymal cells and involved in neuritogenesis
and the cytoskeleton structure.
86
,
89
GFAP is a class III
intermediate filament and a cell-specific marker that, during the
development of the CNS, distinguishes astrocytes from other glial
cells.
90
βIII-Tubulin is a neuron-specific
microtubule required for neuronal axon guidance, maintenance, and
development,
91
which is considered as a
neuronal differentiated cell marker.
The obtained results for
our developed MNG spheroids are similar
to some studies reported in the literature,
92
,
93
showing that the aggressive forms of MNGs are characterized by higher
positivity levels of Nestin, CD133, and Sox2 expression.
83
,
86
4.2
Effects of Pesticide Mixture on Tumor Stemlike
Cells Proliferation and Viability
Histological staining performed
at multiple time points on days 0, 4, and 10 before treatment (
Figure
5
B) enabled target
validation through inspecting tumor spheroid viability and growth.
This protocol was also appropriate for evaluating the cytotoxic response
following chemical treatment (
Figure
5
B).
Based on our data analysis process, pesticide
mixtures may interact to prompt oxidative stress response and mitigate
neural cell density proliferation, leading to the gradual emergence
of apoptotic and necrotic cells. This result, thus, may confirm prior
studies, proving the effect of a pyrethroid on pesticide mixtures
to cause increased toxicity in shorter amounts of time.
37
,
94
Moreover, these pesticides applied in ternary and quaternary mixtures
95
have shown notable synergistic reactions.
Neurotoxicity response was detected at greater doses than the average
daily intake reported for IMD and λ-CYH.
96
,
97
According to the repeated dose toxicity studies reviewed by JMPR
(Joint FAO/WHO Meeting on Pesticide Residues; 2002), two NOAELs (no
observed effect levels) were notably established for the risk assessment
of IMD
98
and λ-CYH on the basis of
neurotoxic signs.
99
Therefore, we can conclude
that the selected highly neurotoxic doses of pesticides make unlikely
any detrimental impact on human health in regulatory environmental
exposures.
4.3
Proteomic Analysis
4.3.1
Assessment of Pesticides-Induced Alteration
on Key Protein Targets in the Metabolic Process
The proteomic
analysis revealed that most of the identified proteins were involved
in the MNG cancer process, exhibiting critical roles in biological
homeostasis and cell metabolism, especially related to binding and
catalytic activities.
According to functional networks and enrichment
analysis, most signaling pathways implicated in the mechanism of cell
apoptosis were predominantly associated with mitochondrial energy
metabolism and redox homeostasis, protein folding and degradation,
cytoskeleton structure and neurogenesis, signal transduction, wound
healing, blood coagulation and hemostasis, and inflammatory mediation
by chemokine and cytokine signaling pathways.
Our results are
similar to our previous study on human high-grade
gliomas for the main identified altered signaling pathways involved
in neuronal apoptosis as well as the significance of protein GO enrichment
analysis in terms of BP and MF.
64
From literature review, one of the major effects of pesticide-induced
toxicity is the metabolic perturbation by inactivation of glycolytic
enzymes, fall in the cellular ATP level, and therefore the rate at
which oxygen is consumed, which may lead to mitochondrial dysfunction
and apoptosis.
59
The most commonly described
proteins involved in the metabolic oxidative stress response are enolases
(ENO1, ENO2), GAPDH, aldolase (ALDOC), and PGK1 associated with glycolysis,
aconitases (ACO1, ACO2) related to TCA (Krebs) cycle, and maleate
dehydrogenase (MDH2) involved in both glycolysis and TCA cycle.
56
In our case study, many key regulatory proteins
involved in energy metabolism were found altered in their expression
profile by down-regulation, namely, aldehyde dehydrogenase family
(ALDH1A1; ALDH2; ALDH1B1.), glycogen phosphorylase (PYGB), enolases
(ENO1, ENO2), aconitases (ACO1, ACO2), superoxide dismutase (SOD),
and aldolases (ALDOC).
To further scrutinize molecular changes
induced by pesticide treatement
with the predicted alteration sites, we have focused our analysis
on three key target proteins, namely, GAPDH, ENO, and PGK1, selected
on the basis of PPI network analysis which allowed investigating all
classes of expressed proteins as well as their degree of relationships,
which helped to highlight the significance of each protein/gene with
its meaningful relationship and regulation.
Following literature,
GAPDH enzymes are a family of largely expressed
oxido-reductases expressed in all prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms,
known for their key role in glucose metabolism, catalyzing the phosphorylation
of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P) to 1,3-bisphospho-glycerate, and
as a multifunctional protein involved in many cellular processes such
as membrane trafficking, microtubule formation as a catalyst, cytoskeleton
organization and assembly, nuclear processes of ribosome interaction,
RNA export, DNA repair and replication, transcription regulation,
phosphotransferase activity, and response to ROS such as a trigger
of neuronal apoptosis.
59
ENOA is a metabolic
enzyme, which catalyzes the interconversion of 2-phosphoglycerate
to phosphoenolpyruvate during glycolysis. It is involved in cell morphology
and proliferation by regulation of the cytoskeletal filament
100
and gene transcription
101
and also known to act as a plasminogen receptor and a heat
shock protein, implicated in many transcriptional and pathological
functions, the alterations of which have been demonstrated in many
neurological disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease.
102
−
104
However, its overexpression was found in more than 20 types of human
cancer
105
explained by the Warburg effect.
106
PGK1 is a glycolytic enzyme that catalyzes
the conversion of 1,3-diphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate. Deficiency
of this protein is also described in many neurological diseases
107
in humans, whereas its overexpression is involved
in cancer cell invasiveness.
4.3.2
Analytical
Validation of the Identified
Protein-Trityl Post-Translational Modification
PTMs are involved
not only in most signaling cellular processes but also in cellular
recognition events and morphology changes that they symbolize changes
in the polypeptide chain as a result of either the addition or removal
of chemical moieties from amino acid residues, the proteolytic processing
of the protein termini, or the covalent cross-links between protein
domains.
The research of PTMs and/or xenebiotic adducts has
received widespread attention for progress in their analysis as putative
predictors of toxicity since they exhibit tremendous potential in
assessing the relationship between exposure to environmental pollutants
and human health risks. In fact, the high-throughput screening and
quantification of these modifications can help clarify the toxicity
and pathogenic mechanisms as well as their roles in human pathogenesis
which enable the early diagnosis of related diseases.
108
However, their analysis is challenging
which highlights the need
for computational and sensitive methods for their detection.
61
,
109
Several research studies in the literature have identified
sites
and type of modifications induced by oxidative stress in the GAPDH
protein, e.g., identification of Tyr-255–adduct induced by
organophosphate Dichlorvos treatment alters the GAPDH function, molecular
structure, and trafficking between the nucleus and cytoplasm, which
consequently leads to accumulation of the altered protein in the nucleus
and thus to apoptosis. Various cysteine modifications were also described,
including S-nitrosilation by nitric oxide, nitroalkylation by nitroalkene
derivatives, thiol oxidation, sulfenic acid formation, and glutathionylation
in response to various oxidative stresses. Oxidized GAPDH on its active
site cysteine residue showed an enhanced binding activity to nucleic
acids.
59
Nevertheless, there are only few

MS represents a powerful tool for the high-throughput screening
of new prognostic biomarkers. It has been steadily emerged in “omics”
studies to qualitatively and quantitatively characterize PTMs with
several advantages, namely, (i) good sensitivity and high efficiency,
(ii) identification of the predicted sites of PTMs, (iii) discovery
of novel PTMs, and iv) capability to identify multiple PTMs in complex
mixtures of proteins, which no other analytical technique could provide.

In fact, the recent examples of MS-based
strategies for PTM mapping
include the introduction of robust high-performance hybrid tandem
mass spectrometery (MS/MS) which provide very high mass accuracy (mass
error <5 ppm) and multistage MS capabilities at a chromatographic
time scale, thereby contributing to detailed insights of post-translationally
modified amino acid residues via peptide sequencing. Moreover, the
multistage MS and efficient fragmentation methods have also facilitated
the analysis of large polypeptides.

Typically,

link between the protein nucleophilic site and the electrophilic form

either endogenous sources (such as oxidative stress) or exogenous

targeted by these reactive species, including reactive functional
groups, at the side chains of amino acid residues.

Conclusions
Pesticide-induced
toxicity in both in vitro and in vivo models
were reported in many published works seeking to ascertain their levels
of safety for general population and occupation hazard. However, few
studies reported the effect of pesticides in mixtures, especially
on neural and glial cells.
Hence, as far as we know, this is
the first finding combining the
use of a human 3D-neuronal spheroid array with an untargeted bottom-up
proteomic-based approach in order to elucidate in-depth the molecular
mechanisms involved in the neurotoxicity effect of pesticides used
in the mixture and to give insights on alteration sites.
Advancment
in proteomics-based approaches with high-throughput
MS technology has helped to investigate in-depth xenobiotic-adduct
formation or protein-PTMs as potential diagnostic biomarkers that
may aid in understanding the pathophysiologic molecular mechanisms
and better plan therapeutic strategies with minimum side effects.
In our study, the proteomic analysis has proved the neurotoxicity
effect of pesticides to induce alteration on sevral proteins involved
in cascading regulatory pathways, mainly on the mitochondrial metabolic
process, which was confirmed by colorimetric methods for the glycolytic
activity. Furthermore, our adaptative strategy on protein adductomics
by the use of a shotgun proteomic-based approach has enabled the characterization
of protein-PTMs and prediction of alteration sites with high sensitivity
and accuracy. Hence, several modifications have been identified in
the active site of GAPDH, PGK1, and ENO1 by de novo peptide sequencing
such as ion losses and adduct formation, particularly a mass shift
of (+242.0 Da) on the C-terminal of 206-Ile residue assigned as a
trityl-PTM and confirmed by manual validation and a colorimetric assay
method.
Thus, our finding provides the first proof that the
neurotoxicity
effect of IMD and
CYH used in mixture was linked to their molecular interaction to
yield protein-PTMs that play a pivotal role in the neurotoxicity mechanism
since they impair the molecular structure, which in turn affects protein
function particularly for those endowed with a crucial biological
role such as our case study of GAPDH, ENO, and PGK1. The study also
offers a broad perspective on how pyrethroids might significantly
increase the harmful effects of pesticides used in combination.
Finally, given the widespread use of pesticides and our investigation
on human health hazardous effects, we support our public health authorities
to be vigilant in the postmarket surveillance of these agrochemicals
and for taking preventive measures with their regular use without
polluting the environment and contaminating food in order to decrease
human exposure risks and provide safer life.
